easy-science-experiments-for-kids:
Each of these has a genuinely unknown answer at the start, which is what separates an experiment from a demonstration. The prediction step is not optional; it is the part where the thinking happens.

Which things float

Predict first: line up ten objects and have everyone guess. Then: a bowl of water. The interesting bit: heavy things that float and light things that sink break the obvious rule, and the child has to build a better one. A ball of foil sinks; the same foil as a boat floats.

Red cabbage indicator

Boil chopped red cabbage, keep the purple water. Add lemon juice, bicarbonate of soda, vinegar, soap. Predict which will turn which colour before starting. Pink is acid, green or blue is alkaline. Children can then test everything in the kitchen, which is the actual activity.

Skittles or sweets in water

Arrange coloured sweets round the rim of a plate, pour warm water into the middle. The colours run inward and stop at clean lines. Predict what happens when the colours meet. They do not mix, which surprises everybody and is worth pursuing.

Which paper aeroplane

Make three designs. Predict the winner. Fly each three times and measure, because one throw proves nothing. This is where the idea of a fair test arrives naturally: same person, same spot, same effort.

The dissolving race

Sugar in cold, warm and hot water, and stirred against unstirred. Predict the order. Change one thing at a time, which is the whole of experimental design in one activity.

Growing towards light

Two identical seedlings, one in a box with a hole cut in one side. Over a week the plant bends. Predict what it will do and why. Slow experiments are worth including because most real science is slow.

Ice melting on different surfaces

Identical ice cubes on metal, wood, plastic, a plate, a towel. Predict the order. Metal feels cold and melts ice fastest, which is a genuine puzzle for a child and leads somewhere real.

The eggshell and vinegar

An egg in vinegar for two days loses its shell and becomes rubbery. Predict what will be left. Slow, dramatic, and it introduces the idea that something can dissolve while something else remains.

How to run any of them

Predict out loud and commit to it. Change one thing at a time. Repeat it, because one result is not a result. And treat a wrong prediction as the good outcome, which it is: you learned something.

An experiment that confirms what everybody expected is the least interesting possible result, and children should be told so.
science-activities-for-kids-at-home:
Science at home is not demonstrations that always work. It is questions with genuinely unknown answers, and most of them need nothing you do not already own.

Questions worth chasing

These are better than activities because they have no supplied method. The child has to invent the test, which is the part that matters.

  • Does bread go mouldy faster in the fridge, the bread bin or on the windowsill?
  • Which spot in the garden is warmest, and does that change during the day?
  • Do all apples brown at the same speed? What stops it?
  • How much water does a plant actually need before it suffers?
  • Which route home is really fastest, and is it the same in the morning?
  • Does the dog prefer one of these two foods, and how would we know?

Every one of them requires deciding what to measure, keeping other things the same, and repeating it. That is the method, learned by needing it.

Observation over weeks

Underrated because it is slow, and closer to real science than anything that happens in ten minutes.

Keep a moon diary for a month. Watch one tree through a year and draw it monthly. Record the temperature at the same time daily. Watch what arrives on a windowsill bird feeder and when.

The learning is in noticing a pattern nobody pointed out.

Kitchen science that is actually science

Baking is chemistry with a deadline. Leave out the raising agent deliberately and compare. Try the same recipe with butter and oil. Whip cream past the point it should stop.

The rule that makes it science rather than cooking: change one thing, keep everything else the same, predict first.

Taking things apart

An old radio, a broken toy, a torch, a clock from a charity shop. Unplugged and unpowered, with a screwdriver.

Nothing needs to go back together. The value is in seeing that the inside of things is comprehensible rather than magic, and children who have taken something apart approach the world differently.

What to avoid

Kits with numbered steps and a photograph of the result, which are craft with a science label. Demonstrations you already know the outcome of, presented as discovery. And answering the question yourself when the child is halfway to it.

The three sentences worth using

What do you think will happen? How could we find out? What would we expect to see if you were right?

Those three turn almost anything into science, including a disagreement about which biscuit is best.
stem-activities-for-kids-at-home:
These are constraints rather than instructions. A constraint has more than one solution and none of them is supplied, which is why it produces thinking where a set of steps produces compliance.

Four to six

  • Build the tallest tower that stays up on its own, from anything
  • Make a bridge two toys can cross, using only paper
  • Sort a handful of objects, then sort them a different way
  • Make something that rolls down a slope slowly

Six to nine

  • A container that keeps an ice cube frozen longest, left outside
  • A boat from foil that carries the most coins before sinking
  • A ramp that makes a marble travel furthest across the floor
  • A structure from newspaper and tape that holds a book fifteen centimetres up
  • A parachute for a small toy dropped from the stairs
  • The strongest possible bridge from twenty spaghetti strands

Nine to twelve

  • A device that gets an egg to the ground from an upstairs window unbroken
  • A water filter from sand, gravel and cloth, tested with muddy water
  • A chain reaction machine with five steps that works three times running
  • Measure the height of the house without climbing it
  • A catapult that hits a target twice in a row, which requires consistency rather than power

Twelve and up

  • Design and cost a real improvement to something in the house
  • Work out the cheapest way to heat one room, with numbers
  • Build something that solves an actual household annoyance
  • Take a broken appliance apart, diagnose it, and decide whether it is repairable

Two rules that make these work

State the constraint, not the method. "Hold a book fifteen centimetres up using only this newspaper" is a problem. "Roll the newspaper into tubes and tape them" is an instruction, and it removes everything worth having.

Let the first attempt fail. Iteration is the actual skill. A child whose first design works has had a less useful afternoon than one whose third design works.

The question at the end

Not "did it work". Ask what they would change if they did it again, and what they learned from the version that collapsed.

That question is the difference between an activity and an engineering education.
engineering-activities-for-kids:
Engineering is not building things. It is building things that have to work, against a constraint, and finding out where they fail. The failing is the subject.

The four things that must hold

Almost every engineering challenge is one of these, and naming them helps a child see the pattern.

Hold: something must take weight without collapsing. Towers, shelves, chairs.

Span: something must cross a gap. Bridges, roofs.

Carry: something must move a load. Boats, trolleys, bags.

Move: something must go, stop, or change direction. Vehicles, catapults, ramps.

Challenges by what they teach

For structure: the tallest freestanding tower from twenty sheets of paper. Children discover triangles and tubes on their own, which is worth far more than being told about them.

For load spreading: a paper bridge across a thirty centimetre gap that holds the most coins. The first design always fails in the middle.

For buoyancy and stability: a foil boat carrying the most weight. Most children learn about width before they learn about displacement, and both are visible.

For energy: a ramp sending a marble as far as possible. Height, angle and surface all matter and can be tested one at a time.

For protection: the egg drop. The classic, because the failure is dramatic and instantly informative.

For consistency: a catapult that hits the same target twice. Harder than distance, and it introduces the idea that reliable beats impressive.

For systems: a chain reaction with five steps that works three times running. Debugging a physical system is exactly the same activity as debugging a program.

The habit worth insisting on

Test, break, change one thing, test again.

Children want to change everything at once when something fails. Holding them to one change at a time is the single most useful piece of coaching available, and it is the same discipline as a fair test in science.

Talk about failure properly

When it collapses, ask where it failed rather than whether it worked. The specific point of failure is the information.

This is worth labouring, because most children arrive believing that a collapsed tower means they were bad at it. An engineer sees a collapsed tower and knows exactly which joint to fix.

What to use

Newspaper, tape, straws, string, cardboard, spaghetti, marshmallows, foil, lolly sticks, elastic bands. Cheap materials are better than good ones because failure is expected and nobody minds.

A child who has built ten things that fell down has learned more engineering than one who has assembled ten kits that worked.
